159.title: The Decapolis Tour
159.b0.ask: “On a tour of the Decapolis without a single miracle, what did Jesus teach about forgiveness, about the Scriptures, and about overcoming evil with good?”
159.b2.p: In Paper 158 Jesus came down from the mount of transfiguration, spoke for the first time of his death and resurrection, and taught that the greatest is the one who humbles himself like a little child. Paper 159 follows the four-week tour of the Decapolis that came next. On August 18 Jesus paired each apostle with an evangelist and sent them out in twelve groups, and they labored in Gerasa, Gadara, Philadelphia, and many other cities.
159.b3.p: Throughout this tour no miracles of healing or other extraordinary events occurred. Instead Jesus visited the groups in turn and taught quietly in the evenings, and his teaching ranged widely: forgiveness, the attitude of a teacher, how to regard the Scriptures, and a positive religion.
159.b4.p: What, then, did Jesus most want to impress upon his followers during this month without miracles?
159.b5.q: ⟦Q 159:1.2⟧In your religion God may receive repentant sinners; in the gospel of the kingdom the Father goes forth to find them even before they have seriously thought of repentance.⟦/Q⟧
159.b8.p: At Hippos Jesus taught forgiveness through the story of the shepherd who keeps up the search for one lost sheep until he finds it. The Father goes out to find sinners before they have even thought of repentance. Since the Father forgives us, we should learn to forgive one another, and Jesus described the steps to take when a brother does wrong.
159.b9.t: 1. Between the two of you alone
Show him his fault with tact and patience
Go again, taking one or two mutual friends
Tell the brotherhood and leave it to take such action as it deems wise
159.b10.p: Believers cannot sit in judgment on the souls of their fellows or forgive sins, but they may maintain temporal order in the brotherhood on earth. When Peter asked whether he should forgive as many as seven times, Jesus answered, “⟦Q 159:1.4⟧even to seventy times and seven,⟦/Q⟧” and told the parable of the chief steward who was forgiven ten thousand talents and then threw into prison a fellow steward who owed him a hundred denarii.
159.b11.p: Jesus taught the dangers of sitting in personal judgment on one’s fellows. Because an individual’s verdict may be warped by prejudice or distorted by passion, he invested legislative and judicial authority in the group, not in the individual. He sought always to minimize the elements of unfairness, retaliation, and vengeance.
159.b13.p: At Gamala John reported that he had forbidden a man who taught and cast out devils in Jesus’ name without following them. Jesus told him not to forbid such a man, and to rejoice that their teaching was already spreading beyond their personal influence. In matters of this sort it is better to reckon that he who is not against us is for us; even a cup of cold water given to a thirsty soul is recorded by the Father’s messengers.
159.b14.t: “⟦Q 159:2.2|153:4.3⟧He who is not with me is against me⟦/Q⟧”
A person’s own relation to the spiritual teachings of the kingdom
“⟦Q 159:2.1⟧He who is not against us is for us⟦/Q⟧”
The outward, administrative relations between different groups of believers
159.b15.p: The man, Aden, did not heed the apostle’s injunction; he raised up a considerable company of believers at Kanata and then went on into Mesopotamia.
159.b17.p: At Edrei Jesus gave the principles that should guide those who teach the gospel. First of all, they must respect the personality of man. Spiritual victories can be won only by spiritual power; people are not to be crushed by the weight of logic or overawed by shrewd eloquence, nor moved by appeals to fear or mere sentiment.
159.b18.t: Do not coerce; appeal to the indwelling spirit, as one who knocks at the door
Restore it to those who have lost it, restrain it in those who have it
A loving father does not frighten his children into obedience
Strong impulses are not necessarily the leadings of the spirit
Uncertainty comes in passing from life in the flesh to life in the spirit
Strong characters do not grow out of self-pity
Believers are not spared trouble, but they need not fear it
159.b19.p: Faith is to religion what sails are to a ship: an addition of power, not an added burden. The believer has only one battle, and that is against doubt. To preach the gospel is simply to teach friendship with God, and they were not to portray their teacher as a man of sorrows; this religion throbs with new life, joy, and good humor.
159.b20.q: ⟦Q 159:3.13⟧I do not promise to deliver you from the waters of adversity, but I do promise to go with you through all of them.⟦/Q⟧
159.b22.p: At Abila Nathaniel quietly asked what the truth about the Scriptures was. Jesus answered that he did not regard them as the rabbis did, and asked Nathaniel not to pass this on to his brethren, who were not yet prepared for it.
159.b23.t: The work of men, showing the enlightenment of the times that produced them
The best collection of religious wisdom and spiritual truth in the world at this time
They also contain much that misrepresents the loving Father
Religious instruction and spiritual guidance, not history or philosophy
Nothing that human nature has touched can be regarded as infallible
The living spirit, not the dead words of another generation
159.b24.p: Jesus told Nathaniel never to believe the records saying that the God of love ordered his forefathers to slay all their enemies, men, women, and children; such records are the words of men, not the word of God. He also explained that they were not writing down the gospel now, lest after his departure they divide into groups contending over its interpretation. The saddest thing of all was that some teachers knew these truths but, as moral cowards, kept them from the people.
159.b25.q: ⟦Q 159:4.8⟧The creature may crave infallibility, but only the Creators possess it.⟦/Q⟧
159.b26.h: 5. The Positive Nature of Jesus’ Religion
159.b27.p: At Philadelphia James asked how to choose the better passages of Scripture, and Jesus named some eternally true and beautiful teachings.
159.b28.t: Teaching to look for in Scripture
“⟦Q 159:5.2⟧Create in me a clean heart, O Lord⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 159:5.3|131:2.7⟧The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 159:5.4⟧You should love your neighbor as yourself⟦/Q⟧”
“⟦Q 159:5.6⟧Neither shall the nations learn war any more⟦/Q⟧”
159.b29.p: Jesus made the fatherhood of God the cornerstone of his religion, and so the practice of the brotherhood of man became imperative. The worship of God and the service of man became the sum and substance of his religion. He put the spirit of positive action into passive doctrines, and he even opposed purely passive nonresistance.
159.b30.t: 2. Suffer evil without complaint or resistance
3. Return good for evil and overcome evil with good
159.b31.p: Turning the other cheek does not mean standing dumb and passive; it means actively leading the brother in error toward better ways. If forced to carry a stranger’s pack for a mile, one should not grumble under one’s breath but carry it a second mile. Jesus revealed a God who goes in search of the lost sheep, turned the negative golden rule into a positive admonition, and brought the philosophy of religion from heaven down to earth.
159.b33.p: The four-week mission was moderately successful: hundreds were received into the kingdom, and the apostles and evangelists gained valuable experience in working without Jesus’ immediate presence. On September 16 everyone gathered at Magadan Park to consider future plans.
159.b34.p: In these dark days David’s messengers kept the believers throughout Palestine in touch with one another and with Jesus, and collected funds to support Jesus and the families of the apostles and evangelists. David even kept an overnight relay of runners between Jerusalem and Bethsaida. Now came a week of rest, the last rest before they reached Jerusalem.
159.b36.p: Paper 159 shows how rich in teaching a month without miracles could be. Jesus taught the forgiveness of a Father who goes out first to find, and told his followers to forgive without limit and to rejoice even in the good done by those outside their circle. He told teachers to respect personality and self-respect and never to frighten people, and he told Nathaniel to treasure the Scriptures as a precious human record while taking the living spirit as the authority of truth. Above all, his religion was not one of passive endurance but a positive religion that actively overcomes evil with good.
159.b37.t: The Father seeks us first, so we must forgive without end
He who is not against us is for us
Respect personality, never frighten, and pass through trouble together
Scripture is a precious human record; the authority of truth is the living spirit
5. The Positive Nature of Jesus’ Religion
Not passive endurance, but actively overcoming evil with good
They learned to work on their own and entered their last rest
159.b39.box: Jesus’ religion is a love that goes out first to seek, a positive religion that actively overcomes evil with good.
160.title: Rodan of Alexandria
160.b0.ask: “How did Rodan, a Greek philosopher who sought the art of living and the way to maturity, come to confess that his philosophy was completed in the gospel of Jesus?”
160.b2.p: In Paper 159 Jesus and his followers finished the four-week tour of the Decapolis and returned to Magadan to prepare for their last rest. Paper 160 records a remarkable series of talks given during that week of rest. On September 18, while most of the apostles had gone home, Nathaniel and Thomas met a Greek philosopher from Alexandria named Rodan.
160.b3.p: Rodan had become a disciple of Jesus in Alexandria through one of Abner’s associates, and he was earnestly trying to harmonize his philosophy of life with Jesus’ new teachings. Jesus did not enter into the discussions himself, but he received Rodan graciously and told Nathaniel and Thomas to listen to all he had to say. This paper summarizes the ten addresses Rodan gave to about two dozen believers.
160.b4.p: What, then, was lacking in a philosopher who had long studied the art of living and maturity, and how did he say that lack was filled in the gospel of Jesus?
160.b5.q: ⟦Q 160:3.1⟧Meditation makes the contact of mind with spirit; relaxation determines the capacity for spiritual receptivity.⟦/Q⟧
160.b8.p: Rodan held that human life consists in three great drives: urges, desires, and lures. Strong character is acquired by carrying each of these to a higher level.
160.b9.t: Where a mature personality carries it
Converted into the social art of living
Transformed into higher longings capable of lasting attainment
Transferred from established ideas to undiscovered ideals
160.b10.p: The more complex civilization becomes, the more difficult the art of living. The true badge of social maturity is the willingness to give up the ease of established beliefs for the pursuit of undiscovered spiritual ideals. Animals make no inquiry into the purposes of life, but man is conscious of the meaning of meanings. Discouragement, worry, and indolence are positive evidence of moral immaturity.
160.b11.p: To solve any problem one must first frankly recognize the difficulty, yet people avoid doing so out of fear, conceit, and prejudice. Only honest and brave individuals can follow through the maze of living to where the logic of a fearless mind may lead. But the greatest of all methods of problem solving, Rodan said, he had learned from Jesus: the isolation of worshipful meditation.
160.b12.p: Rodan confessed that his philosophy had given him the urge to seek the goal of maturity, but that his search lacked driving power and certainty of direction. The new gospel of Jesus abundantly supplied these deficiencies, enhancing his insights and settling his goals. Stability of personality is possible only for those who embrace the living God as their eternal goal.
160.b13.q: ⟦Q 160:1.15⟧Without doubts and misgivings I can now wholeheartedly enter upon the eternal venture.⟦/Q⟧
160.b15.p: The one distinction between man and the animal is that man can communicate meanings, values, ideas, and ideals by means of symbols. Through this ability man develops personality and builds culture and civilization. The most effective of all social groups is the family, and personal affection is the spiritual bond that holds it together. Rodan named four things that friendship and mutual affection contribute to the art of living.
160.b16.t: Many noble impulses die because there is no one to hear them
Pooling insight guards against prejudice and narrowness
Isolation exhausts the soul; friendship enhances the joys of life
Sorrow and defeat lose much of their sting when shared
160.b17.p: He saw the ideal setting for such association in marriage, since Jesus had made the father-child relationship the cornerstone of his gospel. Yet ideal marriage must rest not on the fluctuations of sentiment or the fickleness of sex attraction but on genuine and mutual personal devotion. The same meaning, he noted, lies in the fact that the Master always sends his workers out two and two.
160.b19.p: Maturity requires work, and work requires energy. Where does the power come from? Emotional excitement does not increase energy; it exhausts it. Rodan pointed to the Master, who even then was out in the hills taking in power, and said that the secret lies in spiritual communion, in worship.
160.b21.p: When these experiences are often repeated, they become habits; habits form a spiritual character, and such character is recognized as a mature personality. These practices are hard at first, but once habitual they are restful and timesaving. The mature person wins by tact and tolerance rather than by fighting, for the wise man seeks the key to a locked door instead of breaking it down.
160.b23.p: While the spirit is our goal, the flesh is a fact. The two major problems of life are making a temporal living and achieving eternal survival, and even making a living requires religion for its ideal solution. Rodan listed six essentials of the temporal life.
160.b24.t: Body and mind are the dwelling place of the gift of the Gods
The mind is the mediator between material things and spiritual realities
Ability is inherited; skill is acquired
It requires wise planning and organized channels
Learn to lose cheerfully and never hide failure
Education and wisdom, with wisdom ruling knowledge
160.b25.p: Rodan laid special stress on how to meet failure. Success may give courage, but wisdom comes only from adjusting to the results of one’s failures. False optimism that always claims success ends in the crash of disillusionment. To the God-seeking man, failure is simply an educational episode in the acquirement of wisdom, and a life that looks like a failure in time may prove a great success in the light of eternity.
160.b26.q: ⟦Q 160:4.16⟧wisdom ever dominates knowledge and always glorifies culture.⟦/Q⟧
160.b28.p: Rodan regarded religion as supreme devotion to what one holds worthy of the homage of all mankind. Religion is not mere intellectual belief but a mode of reacting to the situations of life, and anyone who truly has a religion is already its evangel. The supreme ideal of religious loyalty is God, and there can be no genuine spiritual religion without the ideal of an eternal God.
160.b29.t: The ideal of God, a divine reality
Shape God to fit the human heart
Demand that the human heart be changed
160.b30.p: The religion of Jesus not only portrays the Father as the ideal of infinite reality but declares that he is personally attainable by every mortal who enters the kingdom. Rodan called this the highest concept of religion the world has ever known, and confessed, “⟦Q 160:5.8⟧I am a believer, I have embarked.⟦/Q⟧” Yet this way has its price: to be born again and to undergo soul reconstruction, after which comes great peace.
160.b31.p: The impulse to be like God, the emotion of worship, the conviction to serve God, and the reasoning that this religion is best are not in themselves true religion. True religion is a living spiritual experience in which all of these are made personal by the revelation of the Spirit of Truth.
160.b32.q: ⟦Q 160:5.11⟧Just now, our focalized concept of the Father, as held in our hearts, is that God is spirit; as conveyed to our fellows, that God is love.⟦/Q⟧
160.b34.p: Paper 160 is the honest confession of a philosopher. Rodan had thought as deeply as anyone about the art of lifting urges, desires, and lures to higher levels, about the strength that friendship and marriage give, and about gaining wisdom from failure. Yet his philosophy lacked driving power and certainty of direction. In Jesus’ habit of withdrawing alone to commune with the Father he saw the source of that power, and in the gospel of an attainable God he found his goal. Where philosophy stopped, worship began; and when the God of ideas became the living God of the ideal, his eternal voyage began.
160.b35.t: The gospel gave philosophy’s urge its driving power and direction
Friendship and affection make character grow
The power for maturity comes not from excitement but from worship and communion
Wisdom comes from honestly accepting failure
The goal of true religion is not an idea but an attainable God
160.b37.box: The art of living that philosophy sought finds its power in worship and its goal in the gospel of an attainable God.
161.title: Further Discussions with Rodan
161.b0.ask: “How can the infinite God be a person, and how can divinity dwell together with humanity in the man Jesus?”
161.b2.p: In Paper 160 Rodan, the philosopher from Alexandria, set out his philosophy of living. Paper 161 tells what happened after that conversation. Late in September A.D. 29, Jesus left with ten of the apostles to attend the feast of tabernacles in Jerusalem, while Nathaniel and Thomas, with the Master’s permission, stayed on at Magadan for a few days to continue their earnest debate with Rodan.
161.b3.p: Rodan had already been well instructed in Jesus’ teachings by one of the former apostles of John the Baptist, his teacher at Alexandria. So he and the two apostles did not differ over the gospel as a whole. They differed on just two matters: the personality of God and the divine nature of Jesus.
161.b4.p: Can the infinite and eternal God really be called a person? And how could anyone be sure that a man who ate and walked with them was both the Son of Man and the Son of God?
161.b5.q: “⟦Q 161:1.11⟧I am now convinced that, while God must be infinitely more than a personality, he cannot be anything less.⟦/Q⟧”
161.b8.p: Rodan readily accepted all that was presented to him about the attributes of God, but he contended that the Father in heaven cannot be a person as man conceives personality. To him, personality meant full and mutual communication between beings of equality who are capable of sympathetic understanding. Since God is the infinite and eternal Creator, he has no equals, and so, said Rodan, he is transcendent to personality.
161.b9.p: Thomas argued that God does communicate with man, and Nathaniel appealed to his own personal experience with God. Rodan allowed that he had recently had similar experiences himself, but he held that such experiences proved only the reality of God, not his personality. The two apostles asked Jesus to come to their rescue, but the Master refused to enter into the discussion. He only told Thomas that it mattered little what idea of the Father he held, as long as he was spiritually acquainted with the ideal of the Father’s infinite and eternal nature.
161.b10.t: Personality is full communication between equals — God has no equals, so he transcends personality
God clearly communicates with man, so he is a person even by Rodan’s definition
His own personal experience with God
Experience proves the reality of God, but not his personality
161.b11.p: By Monday night Thomas gave up. But by Tuesday night Nathaniel had won Rodan to believe in the personality of the Father, leading him through five steps of reasoning.
161.b12.t: The Father enjoys equality of communication with the Eternal Son and the Infinite Spirit, who are fully equal to him
Jesus, equal with the Father, revealed personality to his earth children, so all three of the Godheads possess personality
Jesus kept up understanding communication with both God and man at the same time
As personality is man’s highest concept of human reality, so God must be a personality
God is the Creator and the destiny of all personality, so he must be a personality
161.b13.p: The third step is the heart of it. Jesus and the Father were one, and Jesus also communicated perfectly with men. Since both God and man understood the meaning of the symbols of Jesus’ communication, both possessed the attributes of personality needed to communicate with each other. Two things which are related to the same thing are related to each other. Rodan then confessed God as a person, on the condition that he might attach to the meaning of personality such extended values as superhuman, infinite, eternal, and universal. And he accepted Jesus as the personal revelation of the Father.
161.b14.q: ⟦Q 161:1.8⟧The personality of Jesus demonstrated the personality of God, while it proved conclusively the presence of God in man.⟦/Q⟧
161.b16.p: One point remained: the divine nature of Jesus, a doctrine only recently announced in public. Nathaniel and Thomas presented their views together, and the book gives their teaching in a condensed and restated form under nine headings. It is less a theological theory than the testimony of men who had watched the Master day after day.
161.b17.t: Jesus admitted his divinity, and the remarkable things of his ministry make sense only if he is the Son of God
The most truly unselfish person they had known, the friend even of sinners, who dared to love his enemies
He never repented of misdeeds; his piety sprang from righteousness, not repentance
Perfect emotional control; just and fair, yet merciful and considerate
He seemed to know men’s thoughts and longings, and was always sympathetic
He knew what happened away from him and asked questions to draw people out
He spoke with the authority of a divine teacher, yet was free from pride
“⟦Q 161:2.9|157:6.11|162:7.6⟧Before Abraham was, I am⟦/Q⟧” — he said that he and the Father are one
He seemed to talk with God face to face
161.b18.p: The apostles held that no mere man would sanely profess to forgive sin. Jesus was either just what he claimed to be, or else the greatest hypocrite and fraud the world had ever known — and they were persuaded that he was what he claimed. Their testimony ends this way: they knew he was human, and they were almost equally sure that he was also divine.
161.b19.p: Strikingly, the first thing they spoke of after his own words was friendship. He made no use of flattery, yet treated them all with equal kindness; he did not hesitate to reprove them, yet it was plain that he truly loved them. The better you know him, they said, the more you will love him. His compassion was moved alike by physical suffering, mental anguish, or spiritual sorrow, and he asked questions to draw people out, not to gain information.
161.b20.q: ⟦Q 161:2.6⟧He prays like a man but performs like a God.⟦/Q⟧
161.b21.p: When their talks were over, the two apostles hurried on to Jerusalem and joined their fellows on Friday, and the other apostles learned much from hearing their experiences. Rodan returned to Alexandria, where he long taught his philosophy in the school of Meganta. He remained a faithful believer to the end of his days and gave up his life in Greece when the persecutions were at their height.
161.b23.p: Consciousness of divinity grew gradually in the mind of Jesus up to his baptism. Once he was fully self-conscious of his divine nature and prehuman existence, he seems to have had the power to limit his human consciousness of his divinity. From his baptism until the crucifixion it was entirely optional with him whether to depend only on the human mind or to use the knowledge of both the human and the divine minds.
161.b24.p: He often withheld from his associates his foreknowledge of events and his awareness of their thoughts. He did not want to go too far beyond the idea of the human that his apostles and disciples held in their minds. The recorders say they saw three ways in which he worked, yet they could not always tell which method he used at a given moment, and they frankly admit that they do not know the full truth about this mystery.
161.b25.t: He acted with only the human content of consciousness
He was seen in conference with the directors of the celestial hosts
The combined personality of man and God working in apparent perfect union
161.b27.p: Paper 161 takes up the two hardest questions about God and Jesus through an honest conversation between a philosopher and two apostles. Rodan believed that the infinite God transcends personality, but Nathaniel pointed to the living bridge, Jesus. Because Jesus communicated fully with both God and man, God is shown to be more than a person but never less than a person. The apostles’ faith in Jesus’ divinity also rested not on doctrine but on what they had seen at his side: his friendship, his blameless life, and his intimate union with the Father. And how the human mind and the divine mind worked together in that one person, the book honestly leaves a mystery.
161.b28.t: The personality of Jesus demonstrated the personality of God
The life they saw at his side bore witness that he was the Son of Man and the Son of God
Jesus could limit his divinity consciousness and used both minds
161.b30.box: God is infinitely more than a person, yet never less than a person — and Jesus showed it in his own life.
162.title: At the Feast of Tabernacles
162.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus, saying that the hour had now come, boldly enter Jerusalem, where those who sought to kill him were waiting, and openly reveal himself?”
162.b2.p: While Nathaniel and Thomas stayed at Magadan to talk with Rodan, as told in Paper 161, Jesus and the ten apostles set out for Jerusalem to attend the feast of tabernacles. They took the shorter route through Samaria. A village on the eastern slopes of Mount Gilboa refused them lodging because they were Jews, and chased Philip and Matthew out with sticks and stones.
162.b3.p: James and John asked permission to call fire down from heaven to devour the villagers, but Jesus severely rebuked them: vengeance savors not of the outlook of the kingdom of heaven. The company spent the night at the village by the Jordan ford and went on to Bethany. Jesus and the twelve then stayed near Jerusalem until the end of October, about four and one-half weeks.
162.b4.p: Everyone knew that the Sanhedrin wanted him dead. Why, then, did Jesus choose this moment to stand in the temple courts at Jerusalem and declare openly who he was?
162.b5.q: “⟦Q 162:7.2|141:7.6⟧You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.⟦/Q⟧”
162.b7.h: 1. The Dangers of the Visit to Jerusalem
162.b8.p: For a long time his followers had begged Jesus to proclaim the gospel in Jerusalem, but now that he was actually going, they were afraid for his life. To all their earlier pleas he had answered, “⟦Q 162:1.1⟧The hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧” Now, to their protests of fear, he answered only, “⟦Q 162:1.1⟧But the hour has come.⟦/Q⟧” His bold appearance at the feast put an end forever to the whispers that he had fled into Phoenicia out of fear.
162.b9.p: There were several reasons why he could teach publicly for nearly a month in the midst of his enemies and still leave alive. These teachings were really the official or formal announcement of the divinity of Jesus to the Jewish people and to the whole world.
162.b10.t: Many members secretly believed in him or opposed arresting him during the feast
Many of the pilgrims believed in him or were friendly to his movement
Their labors throughout Judea had built up sentiment favorable to the kingdom
His enemies wrongly guessed that the Romans had promised him protection
162.b12.p: Asked how he could teach so fluently without having studied in the schools of the rabbis, Jesus answered that this teaching was not his own but His who sent him. Anyone who really desires to do the Father’s will shall know whether the teaching comes from God. The rulers sought to kill him, he said, because his gospel set men free from the burdensome traditions of a formal religion of ceremonies. And he appealed to the people: “⟦Q 162:2.2⟧Judge not according to outward appearances but rather judge by the true spirit of these teachings.⟦/Q⟧”
162.b13.p: The Sanhedrin sent its officer Eber with two assistants to arrest him. Jesus invited Eber to draw near and listen, telling him, “⟦Q 162:2.7⟧I bear none of you ill will.⟦/Q⟧” Eber went back empty-handed and reported, “⟦Q 162:2.9⟧We never heard a man speak like this man.⟦/Q⟧” He even asked the rulers whether they would condemn a man before hearing him. The Sanhedrin disbanded in confusion.
162.b15.p: Early on the third morning of the feast, hired agents of the Sanhedrin dragged a woman before Jesus, saying she had been taken in adultery, and asked whether she should be stoned according to the law of Moses. The book explains that the record we have of this episode is distorted: it was in fact a plot to trap Jesus. The woman’s husband, a man of Nazareth who had shamefully forced her to earn their living with her body, had made a bargain with the rulers’ hirelings to betray his own wife.
162.b16.t: Trouble with the Romans, who denied the Jews the right to inflict the death penalty
An accusation that he set himself above Moses and the Jewish law
162.b17.p: Jesus first walked over near the husband, who stood behind the crowd, and wrote a few words in the sand; the man left in haste. Then he wrote again for the accusers, and they went away one by one; at the third writing the woman’s companion in wrongdoing departed too, and she stood alone. “⟦Q 162:3.5⟧Neither do I condemn you. Go your way in peace.⟦/Q⟧” This woman, Hildana, left her wicked husband and joined the disciples of the kingdom.
162.b19.p: People came to this feast from all the known world, from Spain to India, which made it an ideal occasion for Jesus to proclaim his full gospel in Jerusalem for the first time. It was the feast of the harvest ingathering, held in the cool of autumn, and more Jews attended it than either Passover or Pentecost. At night great candelabras and scores of torches lit the temple, while the Roman castle of Antonia looked down in grim contrast upon the festive scene.
162.b20.t: The people lived much in the open air
A symbol of the seventy nations of heathendom
A symbol of the outpouring of the divine spirit
Water and wine poured into silver funnels leading to the base of the altar
Sheaves of branches and the citron
Waved at the altar while the Psalms were chanted in alternation
162.b21.h: 5. Sermon on the Light of the World
162.b22.p: On the evening before the last day, while the candelabras and torches lit up the temple, Jesus stood up and declared that he was the light of the world. When they charged that a man’s witness about himself cannot be true, he replied that the creature can never sit in judgment on the Creator. His witness was true, for he knew where he came from and where he was going, and he did not bear witness alone but together with his Father.
162.b23.q: “⟦Q 162:5.2⟧I am the light of the world. He who follows me shall not walk in darkness but shall have the light of life.⟦/Q⟧”
162.b24.p: When the Son of Man is lifted up, he said, they would all know who he was, and the One who sent him had not left him alone. Many believed, and no man dared to lay hands upon him.
162.b25.h: 6. Discourse on the Water of Life
162.b26.p: On the great day of the feast, just after the priests had poured the water from Siloam and the wine upon the altar, there was a brief pause after the chanting of the Hallel while the sacrifices were prepared. In that pause Jesus called out: “⟦Q 162:6.1⟧If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.⟦/Q⟧” When the Son of Man has finished his work on earth, he said, the living Spirit of Truth would be poured out upon all flesh.
162.b27.p: He granted that their fathers had done well to keep up this ceremony as a symbol of the outpouring of the spirit. But now, instead of the broken pitchers of ceremonial service, the spirit of the Father and the Son would itself be bestowed. For every one who has faith, that spirit would become the true teacher of the way that leads to life everlasting.
162.b29.p: On the afternoon of the last day, in Solomon’s Porch, Jesus spoke to the believers about true freedom. When some objected that as children of Abraham they were in bondage to none, he explained that he was not speaking of outward subjection but of the liberties of the soul. Whoever commits sin is the bond servant of sin; but if the Son makes you free and makes you sons, you are free indeed.
162.b30.t: Everyone who commits sin — he does not abide forever in the master’s house
He remains in his father’s house — if the Son makes you free, you are free indeed
Not those of his blood, but those who do the works of Abraham
162.b31.p: He sought not his own glory, he said, but only the glory of his Paradise Father, and whoever keeps the word of truth alive in his heart shall never taste death. When they mocked him because he was not yet fifty and talked of seeing Abraham, he said only, “⟦Q 162:7.6|157:6.11|161:2.9⟧Before Abraham was, I am.⟦/Q⟧” Then, as some ran for stones and the agents tried to arrest him, he slipped away to a secret meeting place near Bethany.
162.b32.h: 8. The Visit with Martha and Mary
162.b33.p: While Lazarus and Mary sat at Jesus’ feet taking in his teaching, Martha busied herself with the evening meal. The book explains that she was unnecessarily distracted by numerous needless tasks; that was her disposition. When she asked Jesus to send her sister to help, he told her that only one thing is really worth while, and Mary had chosen it. Yet he wanted the two sisters to learn to serve together in co-operation and to refresh their souls together as well.
162.b34.q: ⟦Q 162:8.3⟧The lesser matters of life should give way before the greater things of the heavenly kingdom⟦/Q⟧
162.b36.p: After the feast Jesus did not teach again in the temple. He divided his time about equally between Bethany and Bethlehem. At Bethlehem he taught Abner and the other former apostles of John the Baptist, and both the courage he showed in Jerusalem and the sympathetic understanding of his private teaching won them over fully.
162.b37.p: So, early in November, Abner and his eleven fellows cast their lot with Jesus and the twelve, and worked with them as one organization right down to the crucifixion. Jesus and his company rested at Ephraim and reached Magadan Park on November 2. The apostles, greatly relieved, no longer urged him to go up to Jerusalem.
162.b39.p: In Paper 162 Jesus no longer waits for his hour. He takes his frightened apostles into the midst of his enemies and openly reveals himself as the light of the world, the giver of the water of life, and the Son who brings true freedom. Yet his boldness never turns toward vengeance or condemnation. He rebukes the disciples who want fire from heaven, speaks without ill will to the officer sent to arrest him, and sends away uncondemned the woman used as bait in a trap. The outpouring of the spirit that the feast symbolized with water and light, he now truly promises. And as he told busy Martha, the lesser matters of life must give way before the greater things of the kingdom.
162.b40.t: Section
Key message
1. The Dangers of the Visit to Jerusalem
When the hour came, Jesus taught boldly in the midst of his enemies
2. The First Temple Talk
His teaching was not his own but His who sent him
3. The Woman Taken in Adultery
Even in a trap, Jesus did not condemn but sent her away in peace
4. The Feast of Tabernacles
The feast of water and light was an ideal stage for proclaiming the gospel
5. Sermon on the Light of the World
Jesus is the light of the world, bearing witness together with the Father
6. Discourse on the Water of Life
Not the ceremonial pitcher, but the spirit itself would be poured out
7. The Discourse on Spiritual Freedom
The truth sets the soul free and makes us sons
8. The Visit with Martha and Mary
Only one thing is really worth while
9. At Bethlehem with Abner
John’s former apostles joined Jesus as one organization
162.b42.box: When the hour came, Jesus revealed himself before his enemies as light and the water of life, yet his boldness always aimed at freedom, never at condemnation.
163.title: Ordination of the Seventy at Magadan
163.b0.ask: “What must those called to be messengers of the kingdom lay down, and where is the true joy of their labor?”
163.b2.p: In Paper 162 Jesus revealed himself openly in Jerusalem at the feast of tabernacles and then returned to Magadan Park. A few days later Abner arrived from Bethlehem with some fifty disciples. Gathered at the camp were the evangelistic corps, the women’s corps, and about one hundred and fifty other true and tried disciples from all parts of Palestine.
163.b3.p: From November 4 to 19 this company received intensive training. Jesus gave a talk each morning; Peter taught methods of public preaching, Nathaniel the art of teaching, Thomas how to answer questions, and Matthew the organization of group finances. From this well-trained group the Master was about to choose seventy teachers and send them out to proclaim the gospel.
163.b4.p: Yet some were set apart as messengers, while others turned away in sorrow. What does it take to become a worker of the kingdom, and where is the true reward of that work?
163.b5.q: “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧Come to me all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.⟦/Q⟧”
163.b8.p: On Sabbath afternoon, November 19, between showers of rain, more than four hundred believers gathered on the shore of the lake of Galilee to witness the ordination of the seventy. Abner was placed at the head of these gospel preachers and teachers.
163.b10.p: Jesus sent them out two and two, as lambs among wolves, carrying neither purse nor extra clothing. They were to stay in a home where those who love peace lived, eat what was set before them, and not move from house to house for better lodging. They were to be as wise as serpents and as harmless as doves. Even when a city refused them, they were to declare as they left that the kingdom of God had come near. Then, as they knelt in a circle about him, Jesus laid his hands upon the head of every man, and the next morning the thirty-five couples set out on a mission of about six weeks.
163.b11.q: ⟦Q 163:1.4⟧Freely you have received of the good things of the kingdom; freely give.⟦/Q⟧
163.b12.h: 2. The Rich Young Man and Others
163.b13.p: Over fifty disciples who sought a place among the seventy were turned down by the committee of Andrew, Abner, and the acting head of the evangelistic corps. Jesus himself never rejected a single person who craved ordination, but more than a dozen, after talking with him, no longer wished to become messengers.
163.b14.t: A disciple who wished to bury his father
He could remain a faithful disciple at home, but the messengers had forsaken all
A disciple who wished to comfort his family first
No man who puts his hand to the plough and turns back is worthy to be a messenger
Sell all that you have, give it away, and come and follow me
163.b15.p: Matadormus, a member of the Sanhedrin, said he had kept all the commandments from his youth. Jesus told him that salvation is the reward of faith, not merely of works, and since he believed the gospel, he was already a disciple and a child of the kingdom. But to become a messenger he must supply the one thing he lacked, and he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. The Master wanted to deliver him from the love of wealth, not necessarily from the wealth.
163.b16.p: The book observes that almost every human being holds on to some one thing as a pet evil, and entrance into the kingdom requires it as part of the price of admission. Years later, after the church at Jerusalem was founded, Matadormus did obey the Master’s word and became the treasurer of that church, but the chance of intimate association with the Master had passed. The forces of the spiritual world will not coerce man.
163.b17.t: Jesus never taught that it was wrong
Incompatible with the spiritual loyalties of the kingdom
Required only of the twelve and the seventy
A legitimate form of insurance against unavoidable adversity
The unfair exploitation of the weak by the strong
163.b19.p: As the young man left, Jesus told the apostles how hard it is for those who have riches to enter fully into the kingdom: no man can serve two masters. When Peter asked who then could be saved, Jesus answered that those who put their trust in riches shall hardly enter the spiritual life, yet with God all things are possible. He did not require all his followers to give up their goods. If one’s wealth does not invade the precincts of the soul, it is of no consequence in the spiritual life.
163.b20.p: When Peter asked what they would receive, having left everything, Jesus promised manifold more in this world and eternal life in the world to come. Then he told the parable of the laborers in the vineyard. Those hired early in the morning and those hired at five in the afternoon all received the same denarius. The householder had broken no promise; he asked only whether they begrudged his generosity because he desired to be good and to show mercy.
163.b21.t: Hired at nine, at twelve, at three
Hired at five in the afternoon
163.b23.p: On the morning the seventy left, Jesus stressed seven points in his last talk with them. Above all, in place of the 613 rules of living expounded by the Pharisees, they were to teach that man’s whole duty is summed up in one commandment: to love God and to love one’s neighbor.
163.b24.t: Proclaim the gospel to gentile as well as to Jew
While ministering to the sick, do not teach the expectation of miracles
Not an outward kingdom of worldly power, but a brotherhood of the sons of God
Avoid overmuch social visiting and other trivialities
Abide in the first worthy home until leaving the city
The time had come to break openly with the religious leaders at Jerusalem
Love God and your neighbor — this is man’s whole duty
163.b25.p: Then Simon Peter took them aside and preached their ordination sermon, urging six virtues upon them. The instruction to “⟦Q 163:1.3|163:4.13⟧salute no man by the way⟦/Q⟧” was simply a common way of telling someone not to waste time on the long Oriental ceremonies of greeting; it had nothing to do with friendly greeting itself.
163.b26.t: Pray for more laborers and do not neglect daily worship
Persecution will come; let those who are afraid step out before they start
Trust the Father for food, shelter, and all things needful
Attend strictly to the Master’s business
Never leave a modest home for a more comfortable one
Seek out the sick in mind and body and help them
163.b27.p: The Jews held the number seventy in special regard, but the book says it was only coincidental that the group numbered just seventy. Jesus would have accepted at least half a dozen others, but they were unwilling to pay the price of forsaking wealth and families.
163.b29.p: On December 6 the whole company of almost three hundred left Magadan and moved to Perea near Pella, where Jesus had been baptized — the same site by the spring where John the Baptist had once camped.
163.b30.p: Pilgrims came daily from all parts of Palestine, from the far reaches of the Roman Empire, and even from Mesopotamia. On his own initiative David Zebedee set up a camp north of the apostolic camp that could receive almost fifteen hundred visitors. Before the seventy returned, nearly eight hundred visitors had already gathered there.
163.b32.p: On December 30 the seventy returned to Pella, and supper was delayed for more than an hour while they told their experiences. At last Jesus could see men spreading the good news without his personal presence, and he knew that he could leave this world without seriously hindering the progress of the kingdom.
163.b33.p: When they reported that “⟦Q 163:6.2⟧even the devils were subject⟦/Q⟧” to them, Jesus told them not to rejoice so much over this, but rather that their names were written in heaven. After a rare moment of emotional ecstasy in which he gave thanks to the Father, the next day he sternly warned the seventy against the subtleties of spiritual pride. If they could understand the downfall of Lucifer, he said, they would solemnly shun all forms of spiritual pride.
163.b34.q: “⟦Q 163:6.2⟧Be not lifted up because of this experience but the rather rejoice that your names are written on the rolls of heaven⟦/Q⟧”
163.b35.p: He closed with an invitation for workers of every age: all who labor and are heavy laden may come to him for rest. Since that day countless thousands have tested and proved the surety of this promise.
163.b37.p: The Pella camp was busy preparing for the last mission, a three months’ tour of all Perea, which would end only when the Master entered Jerusalem for his final labors. Jesus no longer needed to travel far to teach, for people now came to him from all over the Roman world and the Near East.
163.b38.p: The women’s corps had trained a new group of fifty women, who went out with the seventy into Perea. Perpetua, Simon Peter’s wife, was given the leadership of the enlarged women’s work; on the day Peter was crucified in Rome, she was fed to the wild beasts in the arena. The work of the kingdom was now entering a phase of spiritual depth, unlike the miracle-minded days of popularity in Galilee.
163.b40.p: Paper 163 tells of setting apart the workers of the kingdom, and also of those who turned back at the threshold. Jesus forced no one. The problem was not having wealth but the heart that clings to it, and those who would be messengers needed undivided devotion. The seventy who went out came back full of joy, but the Master told them to rejoice not in their success but that their names were written in heaven, and he warned them against spiritual pride. Beneath the whole paper runs the Father’s generosity, which gives the late laborer as much as the first, and Jesus’ invitation to give rest to all who are burdened.
163.b41.t: Freely you have received; freely give — the seventy were sent out two and two
2. The Rich Young Man and Others
The problem is not wealth but the love of wealth
The Father’s generosity gives the latecomer as much as the first
Teach one commandment of love instead of 613 rules
The last headquarters stood where John had baptized
Rejoice not in success but that your names are written in heaven
The work of the kingdom entered a phase of spiritual depth
163.b43.box: The worker of the kingdom, with an undivided heart, freely gives what he has freely received, and his joy lies not in success but in belonging to the Father.
164.title: At the Feast of Dedication
164.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus give the leaders who rejected the light one more chance, and in whom did that light first bear fruit?”
164.b2.p: While the seventy were finishing their first mission and the camp at Pella was being set up, as told in Paper 163, Jesus went up secretly to Jerusalem for the feast of the dedication, taking only Nathaniel and Thomas. Not until they crossed the Jordan did the two apostles realize where the Master was going, and they used every sort of argument to dissuade him.
164.b3.p: But Jesus gave only one reply: “⟦Q 164:0.1⟧I would give these teachers in Israel another opportunity to see the light, before my hour comes.⟦/Q⟧” They lodged that evening at Jericho. At the feast of tabernacles he had sought to reach pilgrims from all over the empire; this time he went for just one purpose — to give the Sanhedrin and the Jewish leaders another chance.
164.b4.p: He knew they would not accept him in the end. Why, then, did he knock at their door once more? And in whose heart did that light first take root?
164.b5.q: “⟦Q 164:4.9⟧One thing I do know—that, whereas I was blind, now I see.⟦/Q⟧”
164.b8.p: At Jericho a lawyer asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, and answered his own question with the law: love God and love your neighbor. Then he asked, “⟦Q 164:1.2|164:1.4|140:8.11⟧Who is my neighbor?⟦/Q⟧” Jewish law defined one’s neighbor as “⟦Q 164:1.2⟧the children of one’s people,⟦/Q⟧” so if Jesus said otherwise, he could be charged with attacking the sacred law. It was a trap.
164.b9.p: Instead of falling into it, Jesus told a story that any Jericho audience would appreciate. A man was robbed and beaten on the road to Jericho. A priest and then a Levite saw him and passed by on the other side of the road. But a Samaritan was moved with compassion, bound up his wounds, brought him to an inn, and paid for his care.
164.b10.t: Saw his sorry plight and passed by on the other side
Saw the man and passed by on the other side
Bound up his wounds with oil and wine and cared for him at the inn
164.b11.p: Asked which of the three proved to be the neighbor, the lawyer answered, “⟦Q 164:1.3|164:1.4⟧He who showed mercy,⟦/Q⟧” so as not even to speak the word Samaritan. He was forced to give the very answer which, had Jesus stated it, would have brought a charge of heresy. The story became a beautiful admonition to all his followers and a stunning rebuke to the Jews for their attitude toward the Samaritans, and it has gone on promoting brotherly love ever since.
164.b14.p: The main event of the visit was a meeting on Friday night at the home of Nicodemus. Some twenty-five Jewish leaders who believed Jesus’ teaching were there, fourteen of them present or recent members of the Sanhedrin, including Eber, Matadormus, and Joseph of Arimathea. Both the hearers and the two apostles were amazed at the breadth and depth of the Master’s learning and insight.
164.b15.p: They proposed ways to win the remaining members of the Sanhedrin and offered to go with him before the seventy. Jesus listened silently, and then told them it would only multiply the wrath upon their own heads without easing the hatred toward him; each should go about the Father’s business as the spirit led. He surmised that most of the Jewish leaders would never accept the gospel, yet he gave them all this one more chance to choose.
164.b17.p: On Sabbath morning near the temple, Jesus saw Josiah, a beggar born blind, and it came to his mind how he might once more bring his mission to the notice of the leaders. Nathaniel asked whose sin had caused the man’s blindness, for in those days such defects were thought to be the result of sin.
164.b18.t: Blindness came from the father’s sin, the child’s sin before birth, or the mother’s sin
Men reap in one incarnation what they sowed in a previous existence
No one’s sin — it came in the natural course of events
164.b19.p: Jesus often warned his apostles to avoid the common tendency to assign spiritual causes to commonplace physical events. Saying that they must do the works of Him who sent him while it was still day, he put clay mixed with spittle on Josiah’s eyes and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam. Josiah came back seeing. He had not asked for healing and had little faith; the book calls this one of the strangest of all the Master’s miracles.
164.b20.t: Not a response to faith, but a wonder he chose for a purpose of his own
There was just enough ceremony to move the man to act
Do not despise or neglect material means in healing the sick
164.b21.p: The prime purpose of working this miracle on the Sabbath, near the temple, was to make it an open challenge to the Sanhedrin. This was his way of proclaiming an open break with the Pharisees.
164.b23.p: The Sanhedrin met in violation of its own rule against meeting on the Sabbath, so that the very court judging an act of mercy as Sabbath breaking was itself breaking the Sabbath. Afraid to summon Jesus, they called Josiah instead, and a serious division arose among the members.
164.b24.p: His parents, afraid of being cast out of the synagogue, admitted only that he was their son and born blind; the rest they left to him. When the court tried a new trap, Josiah answered that he did not know whether the man was a sinner, but one thing he did know. At last, standing on a stool, he declared that if this man were not from God, he could not have done this — and they went straight to the synagogue to cast him out.
164.b25.t: He put clay on my eyes, told me to wash in Siloam, and now I see
What do you say of him?
Whereas I was blind, now I see
“⟦Q 164:4.10⟧Would you by any chance also become his disciples?⟦/Q⟧”
If this man were not from God, he could not do this
164.b26.p: Josiah entered this trial with meager ideas about Jesus. Most of his clever and courageous testimony developed in his mind as the unfair trial went on.
164.b28.p: All through the session Jesus was teaching nearby in Solomon’s Porch, hoping to be summoned, but the Sanhedrin feared to bring him in even as a witness. In the midwinter shelter of the porch, some demanded that he tell them plainly whether he was the Messiah. He answered that the works he did in his Father’s name bore witness for him: his sheep hear his voice and follow him, and no one is able to pluck them out of the Father’s hand.
164.b29.q: “⟦Q 164:5.3⟧As the Father dwells in me, so will I dwell in every one who believes this gospel.⟦/Q⟧”
164.b30.p: Only after hearing that Josiah had been cast out of the synagogue did Jesus go to find him. “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧Do you believe in the Son of God?⟦/Q⟧” he asked, and Josiah said, “⟦Q 164:5.4|158:5.2⟧Lord, I believe,⟦/Q⟧” and fell down and worshiped. He had been cast out of a synagogue, but the Creator of a universe led him forth to join the spiritual nobility of that day. He went with them to Pella and became a lifelong preacher of the gospel of the kingdom.
164.b32.p: In Paper 164 Jesus gives the teachers of Israel one more chance to see the light, though he knows they will refuse it. Yet those who first recognized that light were not the experts in the law. It was the mercy of a Samaritan who drew no line around his neighbor, and a blind beggar who had not even asked to be healed. Under the pressure of the court, Josiah’s testimony grew, and he boldly said that one thing he knew. The leaders cast him out of the synagogue, but the Master sought him out and placed him among his spiritual brethren. Light is never forced; it bears fruit in those who answer it honestly.
164.b33.t: A neighbor is not one of our own blood but the one who shows mercy
Knowing they would refuse, Jesus still gave them one more chance
Blindness is not a punishment for sin, and material means deserve respect
In an unjust trial, one man’s testimony grew
The Master sought out the outcast and set him among the spiritual nobility
164.b35.box: When the leaders rejected the light, it bore fruit in one who showed mercy and in one man who bore honest witness.
165.title: The Perean Mission Begins
165.b0.ask: “What do those who hear the voice of the true shepherd no longer fear, and how should they live between earthly riches and heavenly treasure?”
165.b2.p: Back at Pella after the visit to the feast of dedication in Paper 164, Jesus now entered the last phase of his ministry on earth. On January 3, A.D. 30, Abner, chief of the seventy, gave his associates final instructions and sent them out to all the cities and villages of Perea. This Perean mission went on for almost three months and was the last ministry of the Master.
165.b3.p: During this tour the women’s corps, now sixty-two strong, took over most of the ministry to the sick, and no miracles were worked. No other part of Palestine was so thoroughly worked, and in no other region did the better classes of citizens so generally accept the Master’s teaching. Perea, about equally gentile and Jewish, was the most beautiful and picturesque province of all Palestine.
165.b4.p: In this season, when people gathered for the teaching alone, without miracles, what did Jesus say about the shepherd and his sheep, about fear and trust, and about wealth and treasure?
165.b5.q: “⟦Q 165:5.3⟧Seek the greater thing, and the lesser will be found therein⟦/Q⟧”
165.b8.p: By the middle of January more than twelve hundred people were gathered at Pella. Jesus usually taught at nine in the morning, Peter and the apostles taught in the afternoon, and in the evening the Master held question-and-answer sessions with about fifty advanced disciples. By the middle of March, when he set out for Jerusalem, over four thousand people were coming each morning.
165.b9.p: The Master chose to end his work on earth when interest in his message had reached its highest point in this second, nonmiraculous phase of the kingdom. Three quarters of the crowd were truth seekers, but there were also many Pharisees, doubters, and cavilers. Abner knew Perea well, for it was where John the Baptist had done most of his work, and once the mission began, Abner and the seventy never returned to the Pella camp.
165.b11.p: After the feast of dedication more than three hundred Pharisees and others from Jerusalem had followed Jesus to Pella. With disciples and bitter enemies both present, he spoke in a parable so that each could take what found a reception in his heart. The true shepherd enters the fold by the door; his sheep know his voice and follow him, but they flee from a stranger.
165.b12.t: What he does for the sheep
Enters by the door, leads the way, and lays down his life for the sheep
Climbs in some other way to steal, to kill, and to destroy
Flees when danger comes and lets the sheep be scattered
Claims to see, but the sheep do not know his voice
165.b13.p: Jesus said he was both the door to the Father’s sheepfold and the true shepherd. He had many other sheep not of this fold, and these words were true not only of this world; all would be brought into one brotherhood of the sons of God. No man could take away his life: he had the power to lay it down and the power to take it up again, an authority received from his Father. The next day about half of the Jerusalem teachers professed belief in Jesus.
165.b14.q: “⟦Q 165:2.8⟧I have come that you all may have life and have it more abundantly.⟦/Q⟧”
165.b16.p: On Sabbath, January 28, before almost three thousand people, Jesus preached on “⟦Q 165:3.1⟧Trust and Spiritual Preparedness.⟦/Q⟧” He warned them against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, born of prejudice and nurtured in traditional bondage. They were not to fear those who can kill the body but after that have no more power. Not one sparrow, sold five for two pennies, exists without the Father’s knowledge, and they were of much more value than many sparrows.
165.b17.p: When brought before rulers, they need not worry about what to say, for the spirit within would teach them in that very hour. And to those halting in the valley of decision he said that he had already revealed the Father to them, but he could not lead them to the Father without their consent.
165.b18.q: ⟦Q 165:3.8⟧The Father never compels any man to enter the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧
165.b20.p: A young man asked Jesus to make his brother divide their inheritance with him. Jesus answered, “⟦Q 165:4.1⟧Man, who made me a divider over you?⟦/Q⟧” Then he warned everyone to keep free from covetousness, for a man’s life consists not in the abundance of what he possesses. He told of a rich man who planned to pull down his barns and build greater ones, but that very night brigands killed him, and his heirs fought over what was left. He had laid up treasures on earth, but he was not rich toward God.
165.b21.p: Asked whether it is a sin to possess honest wealth, Jesus said it is not, but it becomes sin when wealth turns into treasures that absorb one’s interests and draw the affections away from the spiritual pursuits of the kingdom. He never approved of improvidence, idleness, or neglect of one’s family; he taught that the material must be subordinated to the welfare of the soul.
165.b22.t: Not a sin — provided your treasure is in heaven
It obscures and even destroys the spiritual vision
It supports the workers of the kingdom, as in David’s tented city
Wealth becoming not your servant but your master
165.b23.p: Asked how the wealthy would fare in the judgment, Jesus said he had come to judge neither rich nor poor; the lives men live will sit in judgment on all. But all who acquire great wealth must answer at least three questions.
165.b24.t: How much wealth did you accumulate?
How did you get this wealth?
How did you use your wealth?
165.b25.h: 5. Talks to the Apostles on Wealth
165.b26.p: That evening, at Andrew’s request, Jesus spoke to the apostles alone. Since they had forsaken everything to become ambassadors of the kingdom, his words to them had to be somewhat different. They were not to be anxious about food or clothing, but to trust the Father, who feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies more gloriously than Solomon.
165.b27.t: Those who give their lives to the gospel shall live by the gospel
They earn their own bread and help support those who teach and preach
165.b28.p: Then, with severe trials ahead, he told them to gird up the loins of their minds and keep their lamps burning, like servants watching for their master to return from the marriage feast. For the Son of Man would depart in an hour and a manner they did not expect.
165.b29.q: ⟦Q 165:5.3⟧Ask for the heavenly, and the earthly shall be included. The shadow is certain to follow the substance.⟦/Q⟧
165.b31.p: When Peter asked whether the parable was meant for the apostles, Jesus answered that in the time of testing a man’s soul is revealed. The tried and faithful steward is set over the household, but the servant who thinks his master is delayed and mistreats his fellows will be cast out in disgrace. Much has been given to them, so much will be required.
165.b32.p: Jesus said his mission would not bring peace in the material affairs of men, not for a time at least; the gospel would divide families and friends. Each believer would have great and lasting peace in his own heart, but peace on earth would come only when all were willing to enter their inheritance of sonship with God. Even so, they were to go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to every man, woman, and child.
165.b34.p: Paper 165 shows how the teaching grew deepest just where the miracles stopped. Jesus stands as the true shepherd who lays down his own life, waiting for his sheep to know his voice and follow. Those who hear that voice do not fear those who can only kill the body; they trust the Father who forgets not even one sparrow. Wealth in itself is not sin, but when it becomes master and swallows the soul, a man grows poor toward God. The Father compels no one, and to those who seek the greater thing, the lesser follows like a shadow.
165.b35.t: Jesus chose to end his work when the nonmiraculous teaching reached its height
The true shepherd lays down his life for the sheep of his own will
Fear not — the Father compels no one
Life does not consist in the abundance of possessions
5. Talks to the Apostles on Wealth
Seek the heavenly, and the earthly follows like a shadow
Trial reveals the soul, and much is required of those given much
165.b37.box: Those who follow the voice of the true shepherd are freed from fear and greed and seek the treasure of heaven, for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
166.title: Last Visit to Northern Perea
166.b0.ask: “If God’s favor is not found in outward forms and prosperity, who will enter the narrow door with thanksgiving, and how are we to understand the accidents that befall us?”
166.b2.p: The Perean mission that began in Paper 165 continues. From February 11 to 20, Jesus and the twelve toured all the cities and villages of northern Perea where Abner’s associates and the women’s corps were working, and found them meeting with success. Jesus repeatedly pointed out to his apostles that the gospel could spread without the accompaniment of miracles and wonders.
166.b3.p: The whole three-month mission in Perea was carried on with little help from the twelve, and from this time the gospel reflected not so much Jesus’ personality as his teachings. Yet the book explains that soon after his death and resurrection his followers departed from these instructions and began to build the early church around miraculous concepts and the glorified memories of his personality.
166.b4.p: What did Jesus teach about outer and inner cleanness, about those who give thanks and those who take blessings for granted, about the narrow door and the broad way, and about accidents that strike for no apparent reason?
166.b5.q: ⟦Q 166:4.10⟧Health is not the smile of heaven, neither is affliction the frown of God.⟦/Q⟧
166.b8.p: On Sabbath, February 18, a wealthy Pharisee of Ragaba named Nathaniel gave a breakfast for about twenty Pharisees and invited Jesus as the guest of honor. Jesus sat down at once without going to wash his hands in the purely ceremonial way, and the host and several others whispered and sneered.
166.b9.p: Jesus told them he perceived they had brought him there not to ask about the gospel but to witness an exhibition of ceremonial devotion to their own self-righteousness. They carefully cleansed the outside of the cups and platters while the inside stayed filthy; they were meticulous in tithing and ostentatious in almsgiving, yet shunned justice, spurned mercy, and rejected truth. To the lawyers he said that they laid heavy burdens on men and took away the key of knowledge — but they could not shut the doors of the kingdom of heaven.
166.b10.t: He exposed their keeping of minor duties while neglecting weightier ones
He likened them to vessels clean outside and filthy within
He saved this rebuke for a later dinner
166.b11.p: Jesus left the house without eating. Some of the Pharisees who heard him became believers and entered the kingdom, but more of them grew all the more determined to catch his words and bring him before the Sanhedrin.
166.b13.p: The next day, near Amathus, ten lepers called out to him from a distance for healing. Nine were Jews and one a Samaritan; their common affliction had overcome all religious prejudice. When Simon Zelotes urged the Master to pass on because of the Samaritan, Jesus said that perhaps the Samaritan would prove more grateful than the Jews.
166.b14.p: All ten were healed as they went to show themselves to the priests, but only the Samaritan turned back, fell at Jesus’ feet, and gave thanks. “⟦Q 166:2.5⟧Arise and go your way; your faith has made you whole.⟦/Q⟧” The apostles all looked at Jesus — all except Simon Zelotes, whose eyes were downcast. The book adds that of the ten only four really had leprosy, and the Samaritan was one of them.
166.b15.t: Grateful for their cleansing, but they went on their way to the priests
Turned back, glorified God with a loud voice, and gave thanks at Jesus’ feet
166.b16.p: Jesus remarked that the children of the house take their blessings for granted, while strangers who receive gifts from the head of the house are filled with wonder and are moved to give thanks.
166.b18.p: At Gerasa a believing Pharisee asked whether few or many would really be saved. People had been taught that only the children of Abraham would be saved, or that only a few would enter, just as only Caleb and Joshua lived to enter the promised land. Jesus granted that the old proverb about the narrow door held much truth, but he gave it a new meaning.
166.b19.t: Wide enough to admit all who sincerely seek to enter
Those who put off entering while pursuing selfish pleasure
It depends on how many heed the invitation
166.b20.q: “⟦Q 166:3.3⟧Even if the door to the way of life is narrow, it is wide enough to admit all who sincerely seek to enter, for I am that door.⟦/Q⟧”
166.b21.p: To those who refused every invitation while the door was open and then sought entrance only for selfish glory, he would say, “⟦Q 166:3.4⟧I know not whence you are.⟦/Q⟧” But every one who sincerely desires eternal life shall certainly find it, and people will come from north and south, east and west, to take the kingdom by living faith. He still stands at the doors of men’s hearts and knocks.
166.b23.p: On the way to Philadelphia, Thomas asked whether spirit beings could prevent accidents. Jesus reminded him that the Son of Man had consistently refused to use the forces of heaven for his own sustenance. The old belief that prosperity was the token of divine approval and adversity the proof of God’s displeasure, he declared, was superstition.
166.b24.p: The Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with the sacrifices, and the eighteen killed when the tower of Siloam fell, were not greater sinners than others; they were simply innocent victims of one of the accidents of time. Jesus then sorted the events of life into three groups.
166.b25.t: Part of the life we live with our fellows on earth
2. Accidents of nature and mischances of men
In no way prearranged or produced by spiritual forces
The harvest of our efforts to comply with the laws governing the world
166.b26.p: A fig tree that bore no fruit for three seasons yielded an abundant crop once the gardener dug around it and fertilized it, complying with the laws of fruitfulness. The Father bestows material blessings without discrimination, but in giving spiritual gifts he is limited by man’s faith and by his willingness to abide by the Father’s will. One hour of teaching will not wholly change the beliefs of a lifetime, and the apostles did not grasp this until after the resurrection.
166.b28.p: Of all the cities of Perea, Philadelphia had the largest group who accepted the teaching of the seventy. Its synagogue had never been under the supervision of the Sanhedrin and so had never been closed to Jesus’ teaching; Abner was teaching there three times a day. This synagogue later became a Christian church, the missionary headquarters for the east, and for centuries a center of Christian learning.
166.b29.p: The book also tells of Abner’s later life. He became head of the Philadelphia church, but he fell out with James and Peter over administration and the jurisdiction of the Jerusalem church, and parted with Paul over philosophy and theology. This estrangement from Jerusalem explains why nothing is heard of Abner and his work in the Gospel records.
166.b30.t: He broke with them over administration and the Jerusalem church’s jurisdiction
He supported Paul’s mission to the gentiles but opposed his version of Jesus’ teachings
They held more strictly to the religion of Jesus, as he lived and taught, than any other group
166.b31.p: Though he lived a life of isolation, Abner lived to be 89 and died at Philadelphia on November 21, A.D. 74. To the very end he was a faithful believer in, and teacher of, the gospel of the heavenly kingdom.
166.b33.p: As the gospel spreads without miracles, Paper 166 clears away one old misunderstanding after another about God’s favor. Washing rituals do not cleanse the inner life; prosperity is not a sign of divine approval; accidents and sickness are not God’s punishments. Thanksgiving came first from a stranger who did not take his blessing for granted. The door of life is narrow, yet wide enough for all who sincerely seek to enter, and whether few or many are saved depends only on how many answer the invitation. And there were those, like Abner, who stayed faithful to that teaching to the end, even in isolation.
166.b34.t: Inner cleanness, justice, and mercy matter more than outward ceremony
The stranger who did not take his blessing for granted was the first to give thanks
The narrow door is wide enough for all who sincerely seek to enter
Accidents and sickness are not God’s punishments, nor is prosperity a sign of his favor
Abner stayed faithful to Jesus’ teachings to the end, even in isolation
166.b36.box: God’s favor opens not to outward forms or prosperity but to the faith that answers his invitation, and the door is wide enough for all who seek to enter.
167.title: The Visit to Philadelphia
167.b0.ask: “In the days in Perea when there were almost no miracles, why did Jesus, on hearing about Lazarus, wait two more days and then set out for dangerous Judea?”
167.b2.p: In Paper 166 we followed the last visits of the Perean ministry. Paper 167 now takes up the days when Jesus went to Philadelphia with ten apostles. At least two of the apostles always stayed behind at the Pella camp to teach the crowds, so as a rule only ten were with him at this time. When he reached Philadelphia, more than six hundred followers were with him.
167.b3.p: These were days almost without miracles. Except for the cleansing of the ten lepers, there had been none on the Perean mission, and the gospel was proclaimed with power, most of the time without the personal presence of Jesus or his apostles. Good news came of the kingdom’s progress at Philadelphia and the nearby villages, and also from Alexandria and Damascus.
167.b4.p: Then, just at this time, word came from Bethany that Lazarus was very sick. Why did Jesus not hurry to him at once, but wait two more days and then, despite his apostles’ protests, head into dangerous Judea?
167.b5.q: “⟦Q 167:1.5⟧Every one who exalts himself shall be humbled, while he who truly humbles himself shall be exalted.⟦/Q⟧”
167.b8.p: A wealthy Pharisee who had accepted Abner’s teachings invited Jesus to breakfast on the Sabbath, along with about forty leading men and a few lawyers, many of them from Jerusalem. A Pharisee of the Sanhedrin made straight for the seat of honor as was his habit, was moved four seats down, and was much offended. Only Jesus’ enemies noticed that he did not observe the ceremonial washing of hands.
167.b9.p: Near the end of the meal a believer suffering from dropsy came in. He did not ask to be healed, but Jesus asked the company whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and then told the man to arise and go his way. Such works, he said, the Father does not to tempt people into the kingdom but to reveal himself to those already in it. Then he taught about places at the feast.
167.b10.t: Take not the chief seat but the lowest place
The host may say, “⟦Q 167:1.5⟧Come up higher,⟦/Q⟧” and you will have glory before the guests
Do not invite only friends and rich neighbors who can repay you
The poor, the maimed, and the blind, who cannot repay you
167.b12.p: To break the silence, a lawyer offered a common saying: “⟦Q 167:2.1⟧Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered with the parable of the great supper. A ruler prepared a great feast and sent for his guests, but they all began to make excuses.
167.b13.t: He had just bought a farm and must go and see it
He had bought five yoke of oxen and must go to receive them
He had just married a wife and could not come
167.b14.p: The angry master had the poor and the outcast, the blind and the lame brought in from the streets and lanes, and when there was still room, he sent out into the roads and countryside until his house was filled. At least one of the sneering Pharisees understood the parable, for he was baptized that same day. The next day the apostles offered many interpretations, but Jesus refused to explain further. He said only, “⟦Q 167:2.4⟧Let every man find out the meaning for himself and in his own soul.⟦/Q⟧”
167.b15.h: 3. The Woman with the Spirit of Infirmity
167.b16.p: For the first time since the Sanhedrin had closed the synagogues to him, Jesus taught in a synagogue. After the service he went to an elderly woman, bent over and bound by the depressions of fear for more than eighteen years, and told her that if she would only believe, she could be wholly loosed from her spirit of infirmity. She believed and straightened up at once. Her affliction was wholly mental; her bowed-over form was the result of a depressed mind.
167.b17.p: The ruler of the synagogue was indignant that he had healed on the Sabbath, but Jesus asked whether each of them did not loose his ox on the Sabbath to lead it to water; should not this daughter of Abraham be loosed from her bondage? The ruler was later deposed and a follower of Jesus put in his place. Jesus often freed such victims from their bondage of fear, but people thought all such afflictions were either physical disorders or possession by evil spirits.
167.b18.t: Mental suffering from fear and depression
Freed her from her spirit of infirmity
167.b20.p: Late on the night of February 26 a message came from Martha and Mary: “⟦Q 167:4.1⟧Lord, he whom you love is very sick.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus seemed for a moment to be in communication with something beyond himself, and then said that this sickness was not to the death, but might be used to glorify God. He loved this family with a fervent affection, but a plan had come to him to give the leaders at Jerusalem one more chance, and he asked the Father’s consent to show his power over life and death.
167.b21.t: Because of the warm climate, the dead were buried on the day they died
The spirit might linger near the body for two or three days
Decay was advanced, and no one ever returned from the tomb
167.b22.p: For this reason Jesus stayed two full days longer in Philadelphia. The apostles were united in begging him not to go into Judea, where the leaders sought his life. But he answered that there are twelve hours in the day in which work may safely be done, and that he would give the Jews one more chance to believe, even on their own terms. Then he told them plainly, “⟦Q 167:4.6⟧Lazarus is dead.⟦/Q⟧” It was Thomas who steadied the others: “⟦Q 167:4.7⟧Let us go also that we may die with him.⟦/Q⟧”
167.b24.p: On the road to Judea Jesus taught about the “⟦Q 167:5.1⟧Terms of Salvation⟦/Q⟧” and told the parable of the Pharisee and the publican. Salvation is a free gift to all who have the faith to receive sonship; there is nothing man can do to earn it. The Pharisee boasted of his righteousness, while the publican beat his breast and asked for mercy. It was the publican who went home with God’s approval.
167.b25.t: Gave the assurance of false spiritual security
Stirred his soul to repentance and confession
167.b26.q: ⟦Q 167:5.2⟧The law of the universe is: Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find.⟦/Q⟧
167.b27.p: That night at Jericho the Pharisees tried to trap Jesus over divorce. He avoided the dispute, but he exalted marriage as the most ideal and highest of all human relationships, and bitterly denounced the lax practices that let a man put away his wife for trifling reasons, pointing out their injustice to women and children. He never sanctioned any divorce practice that gave man an advantage over woman. To the apostles he taught that marriage is honorable, and that parents raising children become copartners with the Makers of heaven and earth.
167.b29.p: The next morning scores of mothers brought their children to be blessed. When the apostles tried to send them away, Jesus indignantly reproved them: “⟦Q 167:6.1⟧Suffer little children to come to me; forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Then he laid his hands on all the children. Those children and their mothers little realized that they were playing with the Creator of a universe.
167.b30.p: Jesus stressed the great value of beauty in leading children to worship. He himself preferred to commune with the Father among the trees and under the starry heavens. A child should first be introduced to worship in nature’s outdoors, and later in public houses of worship that are simple and beautiful.
167.b31.q: ⟦Q 167:6.6⟧Beauty is most religious when it is most simple and naturelike.⟦/Q⟧
167.b33.p: On the climb to Bethany, Nathaniel asked what they should teach about angels, since the high priest was a Sadducee and did not believe in them. Jesus answered that the angels are a separate order of created beings, entirely different from mortals, and that mortal man never becomes an angel.
167.b34.t: A direct creation; they do not reproduce themselves
They are immortal, unless they become involved in sin
They keep one part of creation informed about other parts
Spies who report the thoughts of your heart to the Father
Sure guides of the soul to the mansions on high
167.b35.p: The Father needs no spies, for his own spirit lives within us. Many angels are engaged in the work of saving men and rejoice when one soul forsakes sin and begins to seek God. The talk was cut short when Martha hurried out to meet the Master.
167.b37.p: Paper 167 follows days almost without miracles. Jesus teaches those who compete for seats of honor to take the lowest place, and through the parable of the great supper lets each person find in his own soul what it means to refuse an invitation. He frees a woman bent over by fear, and teaches that the prayer asking for mercy reaches God, not the prayer boasting of righteousness. He exalts marriage, honors women and children, and takes the little ones in his arms. And at the end of all this teaching, knowing his beloved friend has died, he waits two days and then sets out for dangerous Judea to give Jerusalem one more chance to believe.
167.b38.t: He who humbles himself shall be exalted; invite those who cannot repay you
The places refused by the invited are filled with the outcast
3. The Woman with the Spirit of Infirmity
Jesus freed people from the bondage of fear and depression
Jesus waited two days to give Jerusalem one more chance to believe
Salvation is a gift no one can earn; those who seek mercy receive it
The kingdom belongs to the childlike, and beauty leads to worship
Angels are a separate order of ministering spirits
167.b40.box: The feast of the kingdom is always open to those who humble themselves and ask for mercy.
